claim: Deconditioning-update is more effective than traditional extinction in reducing fear responses in rats.
source: Our results indicate that deconditioning-update is more effective than traditional extinction in reducing fear responses
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures comparing freezing behavior between deconditioning-update and no-footshock groups.

claim: Deconditioning-update effects are long lasting and resistant to renewal and spontaneous recovery.
source: Our results indicate that deconditioning-update is more effective than traditional extinction in reducing fear responses; moreover, such effects are long lasting and resistant to renewal and spontaneous recovery.
evidence: The abstract states this claim, supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 2 showing maintained low freezing levels in renewal and spontaneous recovery tests.

claim: Deconditioning-update overcomes boundary conditions for memory updating, such as remote or very strong traumatic memories.
source: Remarkably, this strategy overcame important boundary conditions for memory updating, such as remote or very strong traumatic memories.
evidence: The abstract states this claim, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing effectiveness with 40-day-old memories and 1-mA training protocols.

claim: Deconditioning-update is effective in other types of fear-related memories beyond auditory fear conditioning.
source: The same beneficial effect was found in other types of fear-related memories.
evidence: The abstract states this claim, supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing effectiveness in contextual fear conditioning and inhibitory avoidance tasks.

claim: Deconditioning-update is mediated by L-type voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: Deconditioning was mediated by L-type voltage-gated calcium channels
evidence: The abstract states this claim, supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing that nimodipine (an LVGCC antagonist) prevented the deconditioning-update effect.

claim: Deconditioning-update is consistent with computational accounts of mismatch-induced memory updating.
source: Deconditioning was mediated by L-type voltage-gated calcium channels and is consistent with computational accounts of mismatch-induced memory updating.
evidence: The abstract states this claim, supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5 using an adapted Hopfield network model.

claim: After retrieval, memories may undergo a cycle of labilization and restabilization known as reconsolidation.
source: Particularly, it has been shown that after retrieval (or reactivation), memories may undergo a cycle of labilization and restabilization commonly known as reconsolidation (Nader et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nader et al., 2000, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The labile state induced by reconsolidation can allow changes in memory strength and/or content.
source: The labile state induced by this process can thus allow changes in memory strength and/or content (De Oliveira Alvares et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to De Oliveira Alvares et al., 2013.

claim: Extinction does not erase the original memory but induces new learning that transiently inhibits fear expression.
source: However, extinction is thought not to erase the original memory; instead, it induces new learning that transiently inhibits fear expression (Bouton, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bouton, 2002, representing established knowledge about extinction mechanisms.

claim: Fear memory typically reemerges with the passage of time (spontaneous recovery), exposure to the US (reinstatement), or when the CS is presented independently of the extinction context (renewal).
source: Therefore, the fear memory typically reemerges with the passage of time (spontaneous recovery), exposure to the US (reinstatement), or when the CS is presented independently of the extinction context (renewal) (Rescorla and Heth, 1975; Archbold et al., 2010; Bouton et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Rescorla and Heth, 1975; Archbold et al., 2010; Bouton et al., 2012), representing established knowledge about fear memory recovery.

claim: Reconsolidation has been described in several experimental paradigms and species, from invertebrates to humans.
source: Reconsolidation has been described in several experimental paradigms and species, from invertebrates to humans, suggesting that it might be a fundamental property of memories (Nader and Einarsson, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nader and Einarsson, 2010.

claim: Reconsolidation might be a fundamental property of memories.
source: Reconsolidation has been described in several experimental paradigms and species, from invertebrates to humans, suggesting that it might be a fundamental property of memories (Nader and Einarsson, 2010).
evidence: This claim is presented as a suggestion based on the widespread observation of reconsolidation across species, supported by citation.

claim: Most treatments that interfere with memory reconsolidation are toxic and cannot be readily administered to humans.
source: However, most treatments that interfere with memory reconsolidation are toxic and cannot be readily administered to humans.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge about the limitations of reconsolidation-blocking treatments.

claim: The evidence for the efficacy of reconsolidation-blocking treatments in clinical settings is still limited.
source: Thus, in spite of almost two decades of research on memory reconsolidation, the evidence for the efficacy of reconsolidation-blocking treatments in clinical settings is still limited (Monfils and Holmes, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Monfils and Holmes, 2018.

claim: The transition from reconsolidation to extinction depends on the degree of mismatch between the original memory and the reactivation experience.
source: Research on reconsolidation-extinction boundaries suggests that the transition from one process to the other depends on the degree of mismatch between the original memory and the reactivation experience.
evidence: This claim is presented as a summary of research findings on reconsolidation-extinction boundaries.

claim: Some degree of mismatch or prediction error is necessary for reconsolidation to occur.
source: Many studies have suggested that some degree of mismatch or prediction error is necessary for reconsolidation to occur (Lee, 2009; Fernández et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee, 2009 and Fernández et al., 2016.

claim: If prediction error is too high, extinction may occur instead of reconsolidation.
source: however, if prediction error is too high, extinction may occur instead (Suzuki et al., 2004; Sevenster et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Suzuki et al., 2004 and Sevenster et al., 2014.

claim: When prediction error is low, memory updating/reconsolidation mechanisms are preferentially engaged.
source: Computational models suggest that, in models in which prediction error is low, memory updating/reconsolidation mechanisms are preferentially engaged, as the new experience is recognized as a new instance of the former one
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling studies, representing theoretical predictions.

claim: As mismatch increases, the chances of a new experience being attributed to a new latent cause increases.
source: however, as mismatch increases, the chances of it being attributed to a new latent cause (Gershman et al., 2017) or forming a new attractor in a neural network (Osan et al., 2011) increases.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational models by Gershman et al., 2017 and Osan et al., 2011.

claim: Male Wistar rats were trained in auditory fear conditioning with five conditioning trial tones that co-terminated with a 0.5-mA, 1-s footshock.
source: In order to approach our hypothesis, male Wistar rats were trained in auditory fear conditioning, where they received five conditioning trial tones (CS) that co-terminated with a 0.5-mA, 1-s footshock (US).
evidence: This describes the experimental training protocol used in the study.

claim: In the deconditioning-update group, each tone co-terminated with a 0.1-mA footshock during reactivation sessions.
source: In the no-footshock group, CSs were presented in the absence of shock, while in the deconditioning-update group, each tone co-terminated with a 0.1-mA footshock.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for the deconditioning-update group.

claim: The deconditioning-update group showed a more marked decrease in freezing over reactivation sessions compared to the no-footshock group.
source: Over the course of reactivation sessions, both groups presented a decrease in freezing, but this was more marked in the deconditioning-update group (Figure 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B comparing freezing levels across reactivation sessions.

claim: The deconditioning-update group presented a decrease in freezing of around 70% compared to the no-footshock group in the test session.
source: which presented a decrease in freezing of around 70% in comparison to the no-footshock group and 80% in comparison to the homecage control group in the test session (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Animals in the deconditioning-update group had lower freezing responses in the renewal test.
source: Animals in the deconditioning-update group also had lower freezing responses in the renewal (Figure 1D) and spontaneous recovery (Figure 1E) tests
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Animals in the deconditioning-update group had lower freezing responses in the spontaneous recovery test.
source: Animals in the deconditioning-update group also had lower freezing responses in the renewal (Figure 1D) and spontaneous recovery (Figure 1E) tests
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Memory recovery was not observed in the no-footshock group, possibly due to a ceiling effect caused by insufficient extinction.
source: although it should be noted that memory recovery was not observed in the no-footshock group either, perhaps due to a ceiling effect caused by insufficient extinction
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data regarding the lack of memory recovery in the no-footshock group.

claim: Pre-CS freezing varied between 37% and 69% in both groups throughout the extinction sessions, suggesting some degree of generalization between contexts.
source: Pre-CS freezing varied between 37% and 69% in both groups throughout the extinction sessions (Supplementary file 12), suggesting some degree of generalization between both contexts.
evidence: This claim is based on pre-CS freezing data and represents an inference about context generalization.

claim: When using a 0.3-mA footshock during reactivations, no fear reduction occurred.
source: When performing the same experiment, but with each tone co-terminating with a 0.3-mA footshock in the reactivations, no fear reduction occurred (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The footshock group (0.3-mA) presented higher levels of freezing than the no-footshock group throughout the reactivation sessions and in the test.
source: on the contrary, the footshock group presented higher levels of freezing than the no-footshock group throughout the reactivation sessions, as well as in the test.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fear memory may be strengthened by reactivation with a 0.3-mA footshock.
source: This result is in accordance with a recent study showing that fear memory may be strengthened by reactivation with a 0.3-mA footshock (Ferrara et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ferrara et al., 2019a and is consistent with the experimental data.

claim: The suppression of freezing during reactivations by deconditioning-update is not due to inhibition of delay.
source: It also rules out that the suppression of freezing during reactivations by deconditioning-update may be due to inhibition of delay (i.e. animals learning to freeze only at the end of the CS with extended practice).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the 0.3-mA footshock experiment results.

claim: Deconditioning-update requires several sessions to take place.
source: When using a single reactivation session with 0.1mA, no difference was found in the test in comparison to the no-footshock group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that deconditioning-update requires several sessions to take place.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing no effect with a single session.

claim: Exposure to weak footshocks in a different context without pairing with tones does not lead to fear reduction.
source: In order to test this alternative interpretation, rats were conditioned as described above and the same 3 0.1-mA weak footshocks were given in another context without being paired with the tones (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A). In this case, no fear reduction was found in comparison to homecage controls. (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the devaluation control experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The deconditioning-update effect is not due to US devaluation.
source: We found that the deconditioning group expressed a lower fear level when compared with the no-footshock group in the test even after reinstatement (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E), suggesting that the deconditioning-update effect is not due to US devaluation, but rather to updating of the CS-US association.
evidence: This claim is based on reinstatement experiment data showing persistent fear reduction after US re-exposure.

claim: The deconditioning-update effect is due to updating of the CS-US association.
source: suggesting that the deconditioning-update effect is not due to US devaluation, but rather to updating of the CS-US association.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reinstatement experiment results.

claim: Non-contingent tone-footshock protocol did not attenuate fear expression.
source: We found that this non-contingent tone-footshock protocol did not attenuate fear expression, leading to higher freezing than deconditioning-update during reactivations and in the test (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the unpaired control experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The stress induced by weak footshocks during reactivation is not enhancing extinction by itself.
source: In an additional experiment, we investigated whether the stress induced by weak footshocks during reactivation could be enhancing extinction by itself. Animals underwent either the deconditioning-update protocol described in Figure 1A, or a similar protocol in which both tones and footshocks were applied during the reactivation sessions, but with no pairing between them. We found that this non-contingent tone-footshock protocol did not attenuate fear expression, leading to higher freezing than deconditioning-update during reactivations and in the test (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an inference from the unpaired control experiment showing that pairing is necessary for the effect.

claim: Deconditioning-update is effective in reducing fear in female rats.
source: Next, we asked whether the deconditioning-update effect would also be efficient in reducing fear in female rats. As observed in males, females from the deconditioning-update group showed lower freezing levels throughout the reactivation sessions, as well as in the test session, when compared with the control group (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from female rats shown in Figure 1F-K.

claim: The deconditioning-update group in females had lower freezing in renewal and spontaneous recovery tests.
source: The same pattern was maintained in the renewal and spontaneous recovery tests (Figure 1I and J, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from female rats shown in Figures 1I and 1J.

claim: Deconditioning-update lowers the rate of reacquisition of an aversive memory.
source: The deconditioning-update group had lower freezing compared with the other groups in a subsequent test session in the extinction context, suggesting that our protocol also lowers the rate of reacquisition of an aversive memory (Figure 1K).
evidence: This claim is based on retraining experiment data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Protocols with high training intensity make memory less prone to interference by pharmacological agents in the reconsolidation window.
source: Protocols with high training intensity make memory less prone to interference by pharmacological agents in the reconsolidation window (Frankland et al., 2006; Suzuki et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations representing established knowledge about boundary conditions.

claim: Older memories are less susceptible to modification than recent ones.
source: while older memories are also less susceptible to modification than recent ones (Milekic and Alberini, 2002; Frankland et al., 2006; Suzuki et al., 2004; Bustos et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations representing established knowledge about memory age effects.

claim: Deconditioning-update can attenuate fear expression in remote memories (40 days old).
source: First, we trained the animals in the same protocol described above, but starting reactivations 40 days after conditioning (Figure 2A). Once more, the deconditioning-update group showed lower freezing expression throughout the reactivation sessions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the remote memory experiment shown in Figure 2A-E.

claim: In remote memory experiments, fear expression reemerged in the no-footshock group during renewal and spontaneous recovery, while the deconditioning-update group maintained low freezing levels.
source: However, in the renewal and spontaneous recovery tests, fear expression reemerged in the no-footshock group, while the deconditioning-update group maintained its low freezing levels (Figure 2D and E, respectively; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the remote memory experiment shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Deconditioning-update is effective after stronger fear memory training (1-mA shocks).
source: Next, we tested whether a stronger fear memory would constrain the deconditioning-update effect by training animals with 5 CS-US pairings using 1-mA shocks, while maintaining the rest of the protocol unchanged. In spite of the stronger shock intensity in the training session, the deconditioning-update group still presented reduced freezing levels in reactivation sessions when compared to the no-footshock group (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the strong training experiment shown in Figure 2F-J.

claim: After strong training (1-mA), the deconditioning-update group maintained lower freezing levels in test, renewal and spontaneous recovery sessions.
source: These lower freezing levels were maintained in the test, renewal and spontaneous recovery sessions, in which robust recovery was observed in no-footshock animals, but not in the deconditioning-update group (Figure 2H, I and J, respectively; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the strong training experiment shown in Figures 2H, I, and J.

claim: Deconditioning-update induces a plastic state allowing the fear memory trace to be altered even in boundary conditions that usually constrain memory updating.
source: These experiments suggest that the deconditioning-update induces a plastic state, allowing the fear memory trace to be altered even in boundary conditions that usually constrain memory updating (Pedraza et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the remote memory and strong training experiments, with citation to Pedraza et al., 2018.

claim: Deconditioning-update is effective in attenuating contextual fear conditioning memories.
source: First, we used a contextual fear conditioning paradigm, which is known to involve a set of brain regions that is partially distinct from auditory conditioning and includes the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus (Maren et al., 2013). Animals were placed in the conditioning chamber for 3 min before receiving two 0.5-mA, 2 s footshocks separated by a 30 s interval. On days 3 to 6, rats were reexposed to the same context for 4 min, with those in the deconditioning-update group receiving weak footshocks (0.1mA, 2 s) 3 min after being placed in the chamber (Figure 3A). The deconditioning-update group had lower fear expression during reactivations (Figure 3B) and maintained these lower freezing levels compared with the other groups in the test (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the contextual fear conditioning experiment shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: The decrease in freezing caused by deconditioning-update in contextual fear conditioning is long-lasting.
source: The same pattern was observed in the spontaneous recovery test, performed 20 days later, suggesting that the decrease in freezing caused by deconditioning-update is long-lasting (Figure 3D; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is based on spontaneous recovery data from the contextual fear conditioning experiment shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Deconditioning-update is effective in attenuating inhibitory avoidance memories.
source: Another set of animals underwent the step-through inhibitory avoidance task, in which training consists of applying 4 0.5-mA, 1-s footshocks with 5-s intervals when the animal enters the dark compartment of a shuttle box. During reactivations, animals were placed in the dark compartment for 30 s, with those in the deconditioning-update group receiving 2 0.1-mA shocks. In the test session, the animals were put in the light compartment, and the latency to enter the dark compartment was measured (Figure 3E). The deconditioning-update group showed a much shorter latency to reach the dark chamber (Figure 3F) and spent more time in the dark compartment over the 10-min session compared to the other groups (Figure 3G; Supplementary file 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the inhibitory avoidance experiment shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: The deconditioning-update strategy is effective in weakening distinct types of fear-related memories.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the deconditioning-update strategy is effective in weakening distinct types of fear-related memories.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the contextual fear conditioning and inhibitory avoidance experiments.

claim: The pairing of the CS with a weak footshock is not as effective in accelerating single-session extinction.
source: To address whether the deconditioning-update effect would also be observed within a single, long-lasting extinction session, we trained animals and exposed them 48 hr later to a session containing 12 CSs, with the deconditioning-update group receiving a 0.1-mA footshock at the end of each tone. Fear reduction was limited and largely similar across groups in the extinction session and in the subsequent tests (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), albeit with slightly lower renewal in the deconditioning-update group, suggesting that the pairing of the CS with a weak footshock is not as effective in accelerating single-session extinction.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the 12-CS single-session extinction experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of a weak shock at the end of every CS does not enhance extinction occurring over a single behavioral session, but can actually impair it in the short-term.
source: These results show that the presence of a weak shock at the end of every CS not only does not enhance extinction occurring over a single behavioral session, but can actually impair it in the short-term.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the 24-CS single-session extinction experiment shown in Figure 4A-E.

claim: Activation of L-type voltage-gated Ca++ channels is necessary for destabilizing a reactivated memory during reconsolidation.
source: Other studies have shown that activation of L-type voltage-gated Ca++ channels (LVGCC) is necessary both for destabilizing a reactivated memory during reconsolidation (Suzuki et al., 2008; Lee and Flavell, 2014; Crestani et al., 2015; Haubrich et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations representing established knowledge.

claim: Activation of L-type voltage-gated Ca++ channels is necessary for some forms of extinction.
source: Other studies have shown that activation of L-type voltage-gated Ca++ channels (LVGCC) is necessary both for destabilizing a reactivated memory during reconsolidation (Suzuki et al., 2008; Lee and Flavell, 2014; Crestani et al., 2015; Haubrich et al., 2015) and for some forms of extinction (Cain et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cain et al., 2002.

claim: Nimodipine attenuated freezing decrease in both deconditioning-update and regular extinction protocols.
source: Nimodipine attenuated freezing decrease in both behavioral protocols, suggesting that the drug impaired both deconditioning-update and regular extinction (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the nimodipine experiment shown in Figures 4G and 4H.

claim: Deconditioning-update is mediated by memory destabilization processes requiring Ca++ influx through LVGCCs.
source: In the renewal and spontaneous recovery sessions, high freezing levels reemerged both in the no-footshock vehicle group and in nimodipine-treated animals, while the deconditioning-update vehicle group maintained a lower freezing level (Figure 4I and J; Supplementary file 4). This suggests that deconditioning-update is mediated by memory destabilization processes requiring Ca++ influx through LVGCCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nimodipine experiment results showing differential effects on memory recovery.

claim: Nimodipine injection before reactivations prevented memory destabilization instead of inducing state dependency.
source: We found that animals treated with nimodipine before the test kept expressing high freezing levels, suggesting that nimodipine injection before reactivations prevented memory destabilization instead of inducing state dependency (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on the state-dependency control experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lower degrees of mismatch or prediction error could lead to greater destabilization of stored memories.
source: Computational models using neural networks (Osan et al., 2011) or Bayesian approaches (Gershman et al., 2017) have explored how different degrees of mismatch between stored memories and new experiences can lead to these two outcomes, suggesting lower degrees of mismatch or prediction error could lead to greater destabilization of stored memories.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling studies cited.

claim: A lower degree of mismatch in the reexposure pattern can lead to a greater reduction in subsequent fear behavior than a 'pure extinction' pattern.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, a lower degree of mismatch in the reexposure pattern, caused by weak activation of shock-related neurons (as would be expected from deconditioning-update), can indeed lead to a greater reduction in subsequent fear behavior than a 'pure extinction' pattern (sharing only the tone information with the original memory).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The computational model effect was sensitive to blockade of the mismatch-induced degradation term.
source: This effect was sensitive to blockade of the mismatch-induced degradation term – the model equivalent of blocking memory destabilization mechanisms such as LVGCCs with a drug like nimodipine (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The 'minor footshock' pattern leads to recovery of the original memory as the outcome of the initial sessions in the computational model.
source: This occurs because the 'minor footshock' pattern leads to recovery of the original memory as the outcome of the initial sessions (Figure 5D), causing mismatch-induced updating of the weights supporting these memories and weakening of the mutual connections between shock and context neurons (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: No-footshock extinction leads to immediate formation of a new attractor, leaving the connection weights related to the shock memory unaltered throughout the extinction process.
source: On the other hand, no-footshock extinction leads to immediate formation of a new attractor, leaving the connection weights related to the shock memory unaltered throughout the extinction process.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Deconditioning-update was sensitive to blockade of mismatch-induced degradation in the computational model, while no-footshock extinction was not.
source: Because of this, deconditioning-update was sensitive to blockade of mismatch-induced degradation, while no-footshock extinction – which depends basically on new learning – was not (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Nimodipine did affect regular extinction in the experimental results, unlike in the computational model.
source: A caveat here is that, unlike in the model, nimodipine did affect regular extinction in the experimental results.
evidence: This is an observation comparing experimental and computational results.

claim: The mechanistic distinction between deconditioning-update and classic extinction is not so clear-cut, and these two processes might share common mechanisms.
source: This suggests that the mechanistic distinction between deconditioning-update and classic extinction is not so clear-cut, and that these two processes might share common mechanisms, as has been proposed for reconsolidation and extinction (Almeida-Corrêa and Amaral, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between model and experimental results, with citation to Almeida-Corrêa and Amaral, 2014.

claim: Presenting a tone followed by a weak footshock (deconditioning-update) was more effective in reducing fear memory than presenting a tone in the absence of shock (extinction training).
source: Taken as a whole, our findings demonstrate that presenting a tone followed by a weak footshock (deconditioning-update) was more effective in reducing fear memory than presenting a tone in the absence of shock (extinction training).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main experimental findings.

claim: Attenuation of fear responses following deconditioning-update was robust, long-lasting, and less sensitive to renewal and spontaneous recovery.
source: Attenuation of fear responses following deconditioning-update was robust, long-lasting, and less sensitive to renewal and spontaneous recovery.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main experimental findings.

claim: Deconditioning-update was effective in reducing fear within boundary conditions in which memories have been described to be less sensitive to modification (e.g., very strong training protocols and remote memories).
source: Remarkably, this strategy was also effective in reducing fear within boundary conditions in which memories have been described to be less sensitive to modification (e.g., very strong training protocols and remote memories).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the boundary condition experiments.

claim: Deconditioning-update was effective in other types of fear-related memory (contextual fear conditioning and inhibitory avoidance tasks).
source: The same effect was found in other types of fear-related memory (contextual fear conditioning and inhibitory avoidance tasks)
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experiments with different fear paradigms.

claim: Deconditioning-update was sensitive to pharmacological blockade of LVGCCs.
source: and was sensitive to pharmacological blockade of LVGCCs.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the nimodipine experiment results.

claim: The CS–US association is weakened during the deconditioning-update approach, leading to lower fear expression.
source: We suggest that the CS–US association is weakened during the deconditioning-update approach, leading to lower fear expression.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about the mechanism of deconditioning-update based on the experimental results.

claim: Deconditioning-update is mediated by the memory destabilization effects commonly associated with reconsolidation.
source: Considering that (i) fear reduction is long-lasting, without spontaneous recovery, renewal and savings, (ii) weak-footshock pairings do not have the same effect in single-session extinction protocols or when stronger footshocks are applied, and (iii) this effect is prevented by LVGCC antagonism, we suggest that deconditioning-update is mediated by the memory destabilization effects commonly associated with reconsolidation.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The results are in line with predictions from a neural network model previously built to account for transitions between reconsolidation and extinction.
source: These results are in line with predictions from a neural network model previously built to account for transitions between reconsolidation and extinction with increasing reexposure time in contextual fear conditioning (Osan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim connects the experimental results to computational modeling predictions, with citation to Osan et al., 2011.

claim: Modification of existing connection weights is triggered by a protein synthesis-independent set of processes when there is mismatch between the memory pattern retrieved by the network and the currently experienced sensory state.
source: In this model, modification of existing connection weights is triggered by a protein synthesis-independent set of processes when there is mismatch between the memory pattern retrieved by the network (based on previously learned experiences) and the currently experienced sensory state, as when the prediction of a strong footshock is offset by a mild one.
evidence: This describes the mechanism in the computational model cited.

claim: If mismatch is too extensive, as during extinction in the absence of a footshock, a new attractor is formed in the network at the first reexposure session already, preventing mismatch-induced weakening of the original memory.
source: However, if mismatch is too extensive, as during extinction in the absence of a footshock, a new attractor is formed in the network at the first reexposure session already, preventing mismatch-induced weakening of the original memory.
evidence: This describes the mechanism in the computational model for extinction.

claim: The computational model is able to account for transitions between simple retrieval, reconsolidation and extinction with increasing reexposure time or number of non-reinforced CSs.
source: Although the model is quite reductionist in its implementation, both due to the absence of realistic topology and to the non-spiking, continuous nature of neuronal activity, it is nevertheless able to account for transitions between simple retrieval, reconsolidation and extinction with increasing reexposure time (Suzuki et al., 2004) or number of non-reinforced CSs (Lee et al., 2006; Sevenster et al., 2014), as assessed by the effects of pharmacological agents such as protein synthesis inhibitors, NMDA antagonists and β-blockers.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the computational model with citations to supporting studies.

claim: The computational model helps to explain why deconditioning-update takes several sessions to occur, unlike pharmacological reconsolidation blockade.
source: The model also helps to explain why, unlike pharmacological reconsolidation blockade, deconditioning-update takes several sessions to occur, as the impact of memory labilization mechanisms on a stored memory is much more pronounced when Hebbian mechanisms are blocked concomitantly (Osan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational model with citation to Osan et al., 2011.

claim: The results are compatible with the Bayesian inference framework in which the probability that an experience is attributed to a new latent cause increases in proportion to the degree of prediction error.
source: Although we have not tested this explicitly, our results also appear compatible with the Bayesian inference framework proposed by Gershman et al. (2017), in which the probability that an experience is attributed to a new latent cause increases in proportion to the degree of prediction error generated by previous experience.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about compatibility with a theoretical framework, with citation to Gershman et al., 2017.

claim: A lower degree of mismatch can lead to a greater probability of memory updating and decrease the recovery of fear.
source: This can explain why a lower degree of mismatch, such as that caused by reactivation followed by a weak footshock, can lead to a greater probability of memory updating and decrease the recovery of fear.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Bayesian framework and experimental results.

claim: The rationale for the greater effectiveness of deconditioning-update in reducing fear might be similar to that observed in retrieval extinction paradigms.
